messages.text: I get $2,900 a month in child support and unemployment combined, two kids. Would SNAP help us?

Yes, SNAP (food assistance) could possibly help. Your income looks close to the cutoff, so your rent and other costs will decide it.

**Where you stand (rough check)**
- I'm assuming a household of 3: you and your two kids.
- Child support and unemployment both count as income. Your $2,900 a month is before taxes, which is the right way to count it.
- Search summaries put the federal income limit for 3 people at about $2,960 a month, starting October 2026. That is 130% of the poverty line. You're just under it.
- Reports also say Tennessee may use a higher limit of 200% of poverty. That is still unsettled. If it applies, you'd be well under the limit. Either way, you can still apply.
- A second test looks at your income after deductions. The summaries put that limit at about $2,277 a month. The standard deduction is about $217, which leaves you near $2,680. You'd need more deductions to get under that limit. The main ones are:
  - rent or mortgage and utilities
  - child care you pay so you can work or study
  - child support you pay
- Even if you pass, the monthly amount could be small. I can't give a dollar estimate until I know your housing costs.

**How sure I am:** The official USDA and Tennessee pages wouldn't open for me, so I couldn't check the figures there. They come from search summaries of USDA's 2026-27 update, and sites disagree about Tennessee's rules. Please treat all of this as a rough guess.

**Two questions that would help:**
1. How much do you pay each month for rent or mortgage? Do you also pay heating or cooling separately, or other utilities?
2. Do you pay for child care, or pay child support to anyone? If so, how much?

**Where to apply or get help:**
- Tennessee Department of Human Services: [tn.gov/humanservices](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html). You can apply online or find the SNAP phone number there.
- Dial 211 for free local help.

Only the state agency can decide if you get SNAP. If it looks unlikely after we run the numbers, you can still apply.

rent is $1,200 a month. heating/cooling is separate but i don't know the exact amount, it changes by season. i pay $200 a month for child care while i'm in my job training classes. i don't pay child support, i get it.

Yes, it looks **possibly** likely that SNAP (food assistance) would help. My rough estimate is **about $140 to $200 a month**. That's only an estimate, and it depends on one number I couldn't confirm.

**How I got there (household of 3, income before taxes $2,900)**
- Your income is just under the federal limit of about $2,960 a month.
- I took off a standard amount of about $217.
- I took off your $200 child care, which counts because it lets you attend job training.
- That leaves about $2,483.
- Your rent is $1,200. Tennessee uses a set amount for heating and cooling instead of your real bills, so the changing bills don't matter. I couldn't find that set amount.
- If it's about $300 to $500, the housing deduction brings your income after deductions to roughly $2,000 to $2,200. That is under the limit of about $2,277.
- SNAP pays the top amount for 3 people, **$808**, minus 30% of that remaining income. That gives roughly $140 to $200.
- Without the heating and cooling amount, your rent alone wouldn't be enough. You'd probably be over the limit. So tell the caseworker you pay heating or cooling separately.

**Things to know**
- Tennessee may be moving to a higher income limit, but that's unsettled. It wouldn't hurt you if it happens.
- Your child support and unemployment count as income. If unemployment ends or changes, tell the agency, because your amount could change.
- Reporting your income accurately protects you. Overpayments have to be paid back.

**How sure I am:** I couldn't open the official pages. The numbers come from search summaries of USDA's [2026-27 update](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf). I couldn't confirm Tennessee's heating and cooling amount. The caseworker will use the exact figures.

**Next steps**
- Apply at the [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html). You can apply online or find the phone number there.
- Dial 211 for free local help.
- Only the state agency can decide if you get SNAP.

**Two quick questions:**
1. Do you have savings in the bank? An estimate is fine. Some households have a limit on this, and you can skip the question.
2. How old are your kids? Depending on their ages, WIC or TennCare/CoverKids (health coverage) might help too. Do you want me to check those?
savings are about $250 in the bank. kids are 4 and 8. yeah, can you check WIC and health coverage too? we don't have insurance right now.

Your family has a good chance at help with health coverage for both kids and WIC for your 4-year-old. Health coverage for you looks unlikely, but you can still apply.

**Health coverage for your kids (TennCare or CoverKids): likely**
- Tennessee's [official chart](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html) gives these monthly income limits for a household of 3:
  - **Your 4-year-old (TennCare):** $3,233
  - **Your 8-year-old (TennCare):** $3,028
  - **CoverKids, for kids under 19:** $5,692
- Your $2,900 is under all of these. So your kids look likely to get coverage through TennCare or CoverKids. The state decides which program fits.
- Child support may not count the same way for health coverage as it does for SNAP. A caseworker will work that out.

**Health coverage for you (TennCare): unlikely**
- The same chart puts the limit for parents at **$2,277** a month. Your $2,900 is over that.
- It still might be worth including yourself on the application. How your income is counted can differ for health coverage, and a caseworker needs to look at it.
- If you don't qualify, the application can point you to other options. Dial 211 and ask about plans with lower monthly costs.

**WIC (food help for young kids): likely for your 4-year-old**
- WIC covers kids until they turn 5, so your 8-year-old is too old.
- The income limit for 3 people looks like about **$4,212** a month for July 2026 to June 2027. That's much higher than your income.
- That figure comes from a search summary of a federal notice and a Montana state document. Tennessee's own WIC page wouldn't open for me, so I couldn't confirm it there.
- WIC also includes a short health check.

**SNAP update:** Your $250 in savings is far below the savings limit, so it shouldn't be a problem. My earlier estimate of about $140 to $200 a month still stands.

**Next steps**
- **Health coverage:** apply through the [TennCare and CoverKids page](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html).
- **SNAP:** apply at the [Tennessee Department of Human Services](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html).
- **WIC:** dial 211 to find your local WIC clinic. Your county health department can also help.
- Dial 211 any time for free local help.

Only the agencies can decide who gets coverage or benefits. Report your income exactly as it is. Mistakes can mean paying money back later.

The search didn't turn up a Tennessee heating/cooling standard utility allowance (SUA) dollar figure for October 2026. Here is what the results do cover:

- **Tennessee uses a fixed SUA** for households that pay heating or cooling costs, so the state applies a set amount instead of actual bills. Tennessee offers a fixed Standard Utility Allowance for households paying heating or cooling costs.
- **Federal rules govern how states set these amounts.** A December 2024 USDA memo says states had until October 1, 2025 to make their SUA values comply with the new methodology. State agencies have until October 1, 2025, to ensure SUA values comply with the new methodology requirements.
- **The federal methodology** was designed to set the heating and cooling allowance at the 80th percentile of low-income households' utility costs in each state, with updates each year. The new methodology would set the largest standard, the heating and cooling standard utility allowance (HCSUA), at the 80th percentile of low-income households' utility costs in the State. These figures would continue to be updated annually and reflective of utility costs in each State.
- **Pending legislation:** A 2026 bill, H.R. 7069, would widen access to the heating-and-cooling SUA for households that received energy assistance. It has only been introduced, so it isn't law. Integrates energy assistance into SNAP benefit calculations.
